text: Pillar of Fire is an illuminated glass sculpture located in Washington, D.C., honoring Whitman-Walker Health (formerly Whitman-Walker Clinic) and the healthcare workers who supported people living with HIV/AIDS during the height of the AIDS epidemic. Designed by artist William Cochran of Frederick, Maryland, who specializes in large-scale public art installations, the 16 feet (4.9 m) tall sculpture is shaped like a slender column and represents the ancient tale of a pillar of fire that guided the Israelites through the desert after fleeing Egypt. Composed of 370 egg-shaped layers of float glass with unpolished edges, the column weighs 2,000 pounds and is rigidly post-tensioned to a durable glass and steel rod, placing it under 15,000 pounds of pressure. The glass reflects natural light and is illuminated from within by an internal and external programmable lighting system that responds to changing atmospheric and lighting conditions throughout the day. At night, the color design is an abstraction of the rainbow flag, a symbol of LGBT pride. A plaque on the sculpture’s concrete base states the artwork is dedicated to "Whitman-Walker Clinic and the many health care workers who served the LGBT community in this building from 1987 to 2008, the early years of the pandemic." The lighting system was designed and donated by John Coventry of Chevy Chase, Maryland, with additional materials provided by Acclaim Lighting of Los Angeles, engineering services by New York firm Eckersley O’Callaghan, and assembly and installation completed by Service Glass Industries of Frederick. In 2008, JBG Smith purchased the former Whitman-Walker Clinic building at 1407 S Street NW in the Logan Circle neighborhood. The Historic Preservation Review Board (HPRB) initially suggested a plaque, but JBG Smith, led by vice president James Nozar, chose a more prominent memorial, stating the clinic’s work during the peak of the AIDS epidemic deserved a greater tribute. In 2012, JBG announced the memorial would be installed on the corner of 14th and S Streets in front of the renovated building, which became part of a 125-unit apartment complex called The District. The plan was approved by the HPRB and the Office of Planning and Advisory Neighborhood Commission (ANC), with ANC member Ramon Estrada noting the area is an arts overlay district where public art is encouraged. The total project cost was $80,000. Pillar of Fire was dedicated on November 4, 2013, with Cochran, representatives from JBG and Whitman-Walker, and Councilmember Jim Graham in attendance. Graham, who served as executive director of Whitman-Walker from 1984 to 2009, said the sculpture celebrates the human spirit, particularly the compassion shown to individuals who were often poor, facing a terminal illness, and abandoned by family and employers, who found hope at the clinic. The following month, Mayor Vincent Gray and around 75 people held a candlelight vigil at the memorial on World AIDS Day.
